papers.title: Efficacy and mechanisms of supplementary motor area rTMS for freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease: a randomized sham-controlled trial.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy and neural mechanisms of 10‑Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the supplementary motor area (SMA) for freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease (PD) assessed OFF medication. METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 52 PD patients with FOG were randomized (1:1) to receive 12 sessions of 10-Hz SMA-rTMS (n = 26) or sham (n = 26) over 4 weeks. A total of 50 patients (26 rTMS, 24 sham) were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The primary outcome was the change in the New Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (NFOG-Q) score from baseline to post-intervention (T1). Secondary outcomes included motor/non-motor scales, instrumented gait parameters at T1 and 4-week follow-up (T2), with functional MRI (fMRI) to explore neural mechanisms. RESULTS: At T1, the active group showed a significantly greater NFOG‑Q reduction than sham (between-group difference - 2.36, 95% CI - 3.47 to - 1.25, p < 0.001), with the between-group difference persisting at T2 (- 2.57, p = 0.040). Active rTMS also produced early gains in motor function, balance, and multiple gait parameters, with stride velocity and length maintained at T2. Task-based fMRI revealed enhanced SMA-parietal connectivity during FOG-provoking motor imagery that correlated with clinical and gait improvements. Non‑motor symptoms also showed improvements that were maintained at T2. CONCLUSIONS: High‑frequency SMA‑rTMS produced reductions in FOG severity alongside improvements in gait kinematics and non‑motor symptoms in PD that were maintained at four-week follow-up, mediated by task-dependent enhancement of SMA-parietal network integration. The dissociation between transient motor benefits and retained axial and affective improvements supports SMA-rTMS as a circuit-targeted intervent

papers.title: Oculomotor and Pupillary Biomarkers for Detecting and Staging Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Purpose To evaluate to what degree multimodal oculomotor, vestibular, reaction time, and cognitive (OVRT-C) metrics differentiate Parkinson's disease (PD) from healthy aging and to determine their association with clinical severity. Methods This is a cross-sectional diagnostic-accuracy study, 42 participants with established PD and 24 healthy controls completed a 23-test OVRT-C battery using portable video-oculography between 2023 and 2024. Group differences, age and sex-adjusted logistic regression, and cross-sectional associations with Hoehn and Yahr severity were examined. A parsimonious multivariable model was evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). Results PD was characterized by reduced saccadic accuracy, greater hypometria, impaired smooth pursuit and vergence, increased fixation-instability/nystagmus measures, and altered pupillary responses. The final multiple regression model combined vertical saccadic accuracy, horizontal and vertical gaze nystagmus counts in darkness, and predictive-saccade accuracy (AUC 0.975, 95% CI 0.917-0.995; sensitivity 0.950; specificity 0.870). Performance decreased with LOOCV (AUC 0.940, 95% CI 0.850-0.980; sensitivity 0.875; specificity 0.826). Horizontal saccade latency, vertical smooth-pursuit gain, and pupillary measures were associated with greater cross-sectional Hoehn and Yahr severity. Conclusions OVRT-C-derived oculomotor and pupillometric metrics discriminated participants with established PD from healthy controls, whereas vestibular measures contributed little to diagnostic classification. These findings support prospective validation of OVRT-C metrics as candidate biomarkers for PD and for cross-sectional disease characterization but will require rigorous validation.

papers.title: Dermal α-synuclein seeding in relation to REM sleep behavior disorder across prodromal and Parkinson disease cohorts.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a well-established prodromal manifestation of synucleinopathy and is closely linked to peripheral clinical features in Parkinson disease (PD). Dermal α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) provides a peripheral measure of pathological α-synuclein across these disease stages. We performed a cross-sectional analysis of data from the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), including controls, participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD, and participants with PD. Skin SAA positivity and participant-level kinetic measures (area under the curve [AUC], maximum fluorescence [Fmax], and time to threshold [TTT]) were assessed at 1:20 and 1:50 lysate dilutions. Participants with PD were further classified as suspected brain/motor-enriched or body/peripheral-enriched based on prespecified exploratory clinical features. Skin SAA positivity was detected in 53.3% of participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD compared with none of the controls, and RBD participants showed significantly faster amplification than controls at both lysate dilutions. Within PD, binary SAA positivity was higher in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched than brain/motor-enriched phenotype, but the difference was not statistically significant (83.3% vs 47.6%; p = 0.067). All seven kinetic measures were greater in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched phenotype after false discovery rate correction, but these differences were not retained when RBDSQ total score was removed from the classification. RBDSQ total score was the only clinical variable associated with skin SAA kinetics after correction and was significantly associated with six of the seven kinetic measures. These findings show that dermal α-synuclein seeding is detectable in PSG-confirmed prodromal RBD and is associated with RBD-related clinical features within established PD.

papers.title: Associations between different dimensions of social cognition and apathy in early-to-moderate-stage Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Apathy is a prevalent non-motor symptom in Parkinson's disease (PD), potentially linked to social cognition impairments. However, the relationship between distinct apathy dimensions and multiple domains of social cognition in early-stage PD remains unclear. This study investigated these associations. METHODS: Forty PD patients (Hoehn and Yahr ≤3) and their partners (informants and healthy controls) were included. Apathy was assessed using the Apathy Motivation Index (self- and informant-report). Social cognition covered emotion recognition (ERT), Theory of Mind (SET), alexithymia (TAS-20), and everyday social functioning (OSCARS). Group differences and multiple linear regression analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Moderate to severe apathy was reported in 15% of PD patients, while 32.5% of informants rated the patients as having moderate to severe apathy. Informant-rated apathy was significantly associated with both social cognition and everyday social functioning (R CONCLUSION: In early-to-moderate-stage PD, informant-rated apathy was strongly associated with informant-rated everyday social functioning, partly reflecting shared informant ratings, and more weakly with emotion recognition. Associations of self-reported apathy with alexithymia and social functioning were limited to specific apathy dimensions and are exploratory. These findings support multi-informant assessment of apathy in clinical practice.

papers.title: Assessment of rasagiline as add-on therapy to levodopa for selected motor and non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Motor fluctuations are a disabling complication in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients on long-term levodopa therapy. Rasagiline is a monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitor. It is commonly used as an add-on treatment. This study evaluated the effects of rasagiline on motor and non-motor symptoms. We also examined its effects on quality of life and on serum inflammatory markers. METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled 158 PD patients with motor fluctuations treated with levodopa at our medical facility from January 2022 to January 2025. Patients were categorized into a monotherapy group (levodopa only, n=88) and an add-on group (levodopa plus rasagiline 1 mg/day, n=70). Motor symptoms, non-motor symptoms, quality of life, and laboratory indicators were assessed at baseline and after 6 months. Adverse events were recorded. RESULTS: After 6 months, the add-on group had significantly shorter daily off time (P<0.001) and greater daily on time (P<0.001). Notable improvements were also observed in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III (P<0.001) and Part II (P<0.001), as well as on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (P=0.008), Fatigue Severity Scale (P=0.019), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (P=0.015), and Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (P=0.009). Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores did not differ significantly (P=0.119). Serum neutrophil-to-lymphocyte (NLR) ratio, C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) were all significantly reduced (P<0.001). The overall adverse event rate was similar (P=0.132). CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective observational study, add-on rasagiline therapy was associated with improvements in motor function, selected non-motor domains (depression, fatigue, and daytime sleepiness), quality of life, and reductions in peripheral inflammatory markers. The overall adverse event frequency was similar between treatment groups.

papers.title: Antipsychotic drug sensitivity in Alzheimer's disease due to blood-brain barrier breakdown with considerations for clinical prescribing: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative condition that affects cognitive function, memory and behaviour. Antipsychotics are used to manage psychosis and agitation in AD, through antagonism of dopamine (D2/3) receptors. However, AD patients exhibit an increased sensitivity to antipsychotics that is not shared with patients of other neuropsychiatric disorders. Importantly, older AD patients using antipsychotics show a clinical response and experience parkinsonian side effects at reduced doses with high D2/3 receptor occupancies and lower blood drug concentrations. Consequently, these patients have higher morbidity and mortality risks. A critical component in AD pathophysiology is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), a highly selective cellular monolayer separating blood from parenchyma. This narrative mini-review aims to explore current literature on the role of BBB dysfunction in altering antipsychotic drug sensitivity in AD and the clinical implications to prescribing. We investigate the relationship between BBB dysfunction in AD, involving tight junction protein loss and change in function and expression of transporters, and an increase in brain antipsychotic bioavailability and hypersensitivity. We note that regulatory agencies discourage antipsychotic drug usage in AD through black box warnings and recommendations of avoidance where possible, and only the lowest dose and shortest duration to be prescribed. We conclude that further BBB and receptor occupancy studies in elderly AD patients are essential to ensure a more tailored approach that integrates biomarkers of BBB integrity and drug sensitivity for optimal and targeted pharmacotherapy.

papers.title: Music Beyond Rhythm in Parkinson Disease Gait Rehabilitation: A Mechanism-Informed Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Rhythmic auditory cueing can improve selected gait outcomes in Parkinson disease (PD), but whether liking, familiarity, groove, or personal relevance adds benefit beyond matched rhythm remains unresolved. This mechanism-informed narrative review considers literature published through August 31, 2026 and distinguishes immediate on-cue response, off-cue response, delayed retention, and free-living mobility. Five small, single-session PD gait studies compared music with a nonmusical rhythmic cue while controlling at least tempo. Within-subject comparisons and tempo control strengthen interpretation, but incomplete matching of beat salience, expectancy, instructions, and cognitive demand limits attribution. Findings include acute advantages for selected music conditions and comparisons with no clear difference; nonsignificant differences do not establish equivalence. These experiments do not establish durable incremental benefit. Longer music-based interventions can increase walking during use, but their multicomponent designs do not isolate music from rhythm, adaptation, or feedback. No included study demonstrated a music-specific mediated effect on gait or established prospective mediation from liking through engagement and practice dose to retention. Evidence for auditory cueing as an intervention should therefore be distinguished from proof of a shared rhythmic causal mechanism. Incremental music-associated benefits remain possible and require rhythm-matched longitudinal comparisons and temporally ordered process measurements.

papers.title: Long-term implications of appendectomy in children: reappraising the appendix as a functional organ.
papers.abstract: Appendectomy is among the most frequently performed operations in children, and acute appendicitis remains one of the most common pediatric surgical emergencies worldwide. For more than a century, the appendix was regarded as a vestigial structure whose removal carried no lasting consequence, an assumption that underlies the long-standing default of operative management of appendicitis. Two developments now invite reexamination of that assumption: the growing use of nonoperative management for uncomplicated appendicitis, and an expanding body of evidence arguing the appendix is immunologically active and serves as a reservoir for the gut microbiome. This review synthesizes current data on the long-term implications of appendectomy in the pediatric population. We first examine the appendix as a functional organ-its immunologic role, its function as a microbiome reservoir, and its participation in the gut-brain axis. We review its proposed associations with inflammatory bowel disease, systemic autoimmune disease, and Parkinson disease, followed by its oncologic relevance with respect to appendiceal neuroendocrine tumors and colorectal cancer. Much of the evidence is observational, derived from adults, and contradictory. Appendectomy for appropriate indications remains safe and effective, but increasing understanding of the appendix's biology and consequences of its removal may be helpful with shared decision-making.

papers.title: Self-reported dysphagia among community-dwelling adults with Parkinson's disease: A retrospective analysis of fox insight data.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Dysphagia in Parkinson's disease (PD) is common but variably defined. We estimated the prevalence, associated factors, adverse outcomes, and patient-reported burden among community-dwelling adults with PD. METHODS: We conducted a secondary analysis of Fox Insight, an online longitudinal cohort. The primary association outcome was ever reporting difficulty swallowing food or drink, or choking, in the past month. First available and most recent responses provided single-response estimates. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors, with questionnaire-count adjustment in a sensitivity analysis. RESULTS: Among 43,833 participants, 31,243 were in the self-reported PD/parkinsonism group. 31.8% reported swallowing symptoms at the first response, 40.8% at the most recent response, and 56.9% at least once during follow-up (versus 27.3% without PD). Participants ever reporting dysphagia completed more questionnaires (median 6 vs 2). In adjusted analyses, dysphagia was associated with mid-duration PD (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.11-1.24), later-duration disease (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.31-1.54), GERD (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.45-1.63), traumatic brain injury (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.33-1.60), lung disease, heart disease, and stroke. Associations persisted after adjustment for questionnaire count, although estimates changed. In unadjusted comparisons, adverse outcomes were more frequently reported. Among participants with swallowing-specific quality of life data (n CONCLUSION: Self-reported dysphagia was common, but estimates depend on symptom classification and observation opportunity. By linking symptom reporting with consistent clinical associations and patient-perceived burden, these findings build on prior research and support more proactive recognition of swallowing symptoms in community-dwelling adults with PD.

papers.title: The Genetic Architecture of Essential Tremor.
papers.journal: Tremor and other hyperkinetic movements (New York, N.Y.)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Essential tremor (ET) is the most common adult movement disorder with a reported global prevalence of 0.32%-0.9%, rising to 4.6-6.3% in those >65 years [12345]. Autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance have been reported in some multiplex ET families; genetic studies continue to yield heterogenous results [67]. Despite numerous reported genes and loci, replication has been inconsistent and the relative strength of genetic findings varies considerably [89]. OBJECTIVE: To provide a comprehensive overview of advances in ET genetics over the last decade, synthesising evidence across contemporary genetic approaches and identifying key gaps and priorities for future research. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for human genetic studies of ET published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included candidate-gene, genome-wide association, family-based sequencing and other genomic approaches. Following screening and hand-searching of reference lists, 33 studies were included. RESULTS: Genetic findings were highly heterogeneous. Evidence included common susceptibility loci with small effects, rare family-specific variants, repeat expansions and candidate-gene associations, but independent replication was limited. Most studies also used diagnostic criteria predating the 2018 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society (IPMDS) tremor classification. DISCUSSION: Current evidence supports a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture for ET rather than a single genetic model. Larger ancestry-diverse cohorts, consistent longitudinal phenotyping, independent replication and integration of genomic findings with functional and molecular approaches are required to establish biologically and clinically relevant genetic determinants.
